q: Calculate how many times more species there are in Carex than in Canis.
2000 / 7 = about 290 times.
Explain why a genus is not a fixed unit like a metre.
Genera are set by taxonomists’ judgement; there is no agreed rule for how different species must be to share a genus, so genera vary greatly between groups.
Suggest why sedges and fruit flies have so many species.
Any two: many different habitats and niches; short generation times; populations easily isolated, so speciation is frequent.
Humans and chimpanzees are placed in different genera. Discuss whether they should be.

Genetically they are very close (98.8%), and in many other groups species this similar share a genus. Keeping humans separate may reflect tradition and human-centred thinking. Cladistics would focus on the shared ancestor, not the rank.
Explain what cladistics uses instead of ranks.
Clades: groups made of a common ancestor and all its descendants, identified from shared derived characters or sequences.

18.t: Working with data: building a cladogram
q: Identify the two pairs of species that are most closely related.
V and W (2 differences) and Y and Z (4 differences).
Describe the cladogram these data support.
V and W are sister species; X branches off just before them; Y and Z form a second clade; the two clades meet at the root: ((V, W), X) and (Y, Z).
Estimate how long ago V and W shared a common ancestor.
2 differences × 5 million years = about 10 million years.
State one assumption of this method and one reason it could give a wrong answer.
Assumes a constant rate of change. It could fail because rates differ between genes and lineages, or the same base changes twice (back mutation).
Explain why a tree based on one short sequence may be unreliable.
With few differences, chance has a big effect; other genes may give a different tree.
